title: I played Android’s first AI frame-gen game: Mobile just had its DLSS moment
summary: Like it or not, AI upscaling is the future of mobile gaming.
body: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority Talk of the mobile silicon town this year is, once again, AI, but this time with a twist for gamers. The latest GPU developments from Arm and Qualcomm center on similar neural upscaling techniques we’ve long seen in the PC space, using “AI” to boost frame rates and resolutions, making next-gen games look and run better without the traditional rendering costs. In a bid to showcase that this is more than just tech demo talk, Arm worked closely with developer Sumo Digital to create Neural Dawn — a light platforming title built from the ground up to use Unreal Engine’s impressive MegaLights ray-traced lighting system. The game leverages Arm’s Neural Super Sampling and Denoising (NSSD) and Neural Frame Rate Upscaling (NFRU) technologies to make this actually run on a smartphone. Version 1.0 just dropped last week, meaning we can actually go and play it.

title: Google wants to lock Android down, but Droynis teaches you how to stay safe instead
summary: Droynis keeps me accountable for the security settings I select.
body: Part of the beauty of Android is its openness. It’s one of the many reasons why I would rather snag a Pixel or Galaxy device ahead of an iPhone. I can choose which default apps to employ, where I get them from, how I set up my phone, and even circumvent some restrictions if I’m feeling particularly spicy. A shortcoming of this borderless design is that Android users can often inadvertently set up an environment with potential security issues. As is so often the case with Android, that particular problem also breeds opportunity, and a new open-source app has jumped in to help Google solve it. It’s called Droynis , and it’s the security auditing tool that should’ve been a part of Android all along.
